Introduction The Last Glacial Maximum (LGM, ~ 21 ka BP) was the peak of the most recent glaciation and marked the critical threshold for the global transition from glacial to interglacial conditions 1 .
Although the Holocene brought generally warmer and more stable conditions, abrupt climate fluctuations persisted on millennial–centennial timescales.
The Yangtze River Delta (YRD), located at the land–sea transition of the East Asian summer monsoon (EASM) domain, provides high-resolution archives of past environmental change.
As one of China’s most densely populated and economically dynamic regions, understanding the paleoclimate history of YRD is essential for assessing regional climate resilience.
The region is characterized by low-lying plains (< 5 m a.s.l.) and a subtropical monsoon climate, with mean annual temperature of 14–18 °C and precipitation of 1100–1400 mm.
Its modern landscape reflects strong fluvial–tidal interactions, with the Yangtze River delivering about 4.8 × 10⁸ t of suspended sediment annually.

The CSJA6 core (Nantong, Jiangsu) also records seven stages: 19.0–18.0 ka was cold–dry, 18.0–12.9 ka saw gradual warming with precipitation decreasing and then increasing (transition to warm–humid), 12.9–10.9 ka was warm–dry, 10.9–7.9 ka was warm–humid, 7.9–5.4 ka was relatively warm–dry, 5.4–1.6 ka was cold–dry, and after 1.6 ka, warming and subsequent cooling with increasing precipitation reflected a relatively cool climate.

Overall, although the three sites differ in the exact timing and intensity of changes, they consistently demonstrate multistage climatic fluctuations since the LGM, which is broadly consistent with major East Asian climate transitions.

Tann and Pann from LZK1 and CSJA6 are statistically significant ( p < 0.05), MTwa from CSJA6 provides reference information, and the overall trends align with ecological expectations (see Supplementary Materials Section S4).

During the B/A (14.7–12.9 ka), the conditions shifted to warm and humid (T ann >15 °C, P ann >1200 mm), with evergreen–deciduous broadleaf forest ( Quercus up to 30%), clay–silt > 80%, and magnetic susceptibility < 40 × 10⁻⁸ SI, which is consistent with ~ 60 m sea-level rise 23 .

The YD (12.9–11.7 ka) produced abrupt cooling (Tann drop ~ 2.2 °C), P ann fluctuations ~ 400 mm, vegetation shift to deciduous broadleaf forest–meadow (Poaceae up to 30%), sand content rising to 40–80%, and magnetic susceptibility exceeding 80 × 10⁻⁸ SI, in phase with Greenland ice-core and North Atlantic coral δ¹⁸O records 24 , 25 , suggesting a possible link to AMOC disruption 26 .

The early Holocene (11.7–8.2 ka) was the warmest and wettest period since the LGM (T ann ~15.2 °C, P ann ~1200 mm, MT wa ~31.1 °C).

The 8.2 ka event (8.2–7.8 ka) saw rapid T ann decline from 15.2 to 12.7 °C, with P ann increasing by ~ 300 mm, consistent with freshwater input into the North Atlantic, potential AMOC weakening, and southward Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) shift 28 , 29 .

During the mid-Holocene (8.2–4.2 ka), warm‒humid conditions continued (T ann ~15.3 °C, P ann ~1170 mm, MT wa ~30.3 °C), with evergreen–deciduous broadleaf forest and strongly fluctuating sand content.

6 ), the driving mechanisms of the EASM clearly differ across temporal scales, with millennial- and centennial-scale variations controlled by distinct factors under the combined influence of external forcing and internal feedbacks.

AMOC acted as a key interhemispheric link, with its weakening associated with the YD and 8.2 ka cold events 28 , 29 , 54 , 55 , while its recovery during the B/A period enhanced the EASM 56 .

During deglaciation, rapid sea-level rise (e.g., ~ 60 m in the B/A) altered land–sea configurations and atmospheric circulation 53 , potentially promoting EASM strengthening and forming a positive feedback loop of “ice-sheet melting–sea-level rise–monsoon intensification.” At the centennial scale, the EASM variability was probably more strongly modulated by solar activity cycles, volcanic eruptions, and ocean–atmosphere modes such as ENSO 62 .

Quantitative reconstruction models Prior to reconstruction, pollen data were square-root transformed to stabilize variance.

Six transfer function approaches were tested: Modern Analogue Technique (MAT), Weighted Averaging (WA), Weighted Averaging Partial Least Squares (WAPLS), Locally-Weighted Weighted-Averaging (LWWA), Locally-Weighted Weighted-Averaging Partial Least Squares (LWWAPLS), and Random Forests.
